text.hook:
weak_ptr has no operator->, no get(), no *.
That is not a missing feature. It is the whole design.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Owning vs observing
2. The weak_ptr API contract
3. Object vs control block lifetime
4. Which link becomes weak, enable_shared_from_this
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Observing without owning, breaking cycles, and the answers that fail.

slides.title: Owning vs observing

cards.label: shared_ptr
cards.text: "I own this. While I exist, it stays alive."

cards.label: weak_ptr
cards.text: "I observe this. I do not keep it alive."

cards.label: lock()
cards.text: To touch the object, become an owner for a moment: a `shared_ptr`, or empty if it is gone.

slides.takeaway: A `weak_ptr` keeps the **control block** alive, never the object.

slides.title: What each call really does
rows: `shared_ptr`, or empty if expired. Never throws
the **strong** count, not the weak one
do not exist: it does not compile
slides.takeaway: No constructor from a raw pointer: a `weak_ptr` always comes from a `shared_ptr`.

slides.title: `p.reset()` with a `weak_ptr` watching
steps: Strong count 1 ➜ 0: the object is destroyed **right there**
The control block survives, so `w.expired()` can say `true`
`w.lock()` returns empty. A dead object never comes back
`w` destroyed: weak count 0, control block freed

slides.title: Which link becomes weak?
slides.takeaway: Strong edges must form a tree. Make the wrong edge weak and the owner stops keeping its child alive.

cards.label: The problem
cards.text: A member function needs a `shared_ptr` to its own object, but only has `this`.

cards.label: The bug
cards.text: `shared_ptr<T>(this)`: a **second** control block, so a double delete.

cards.label: The fix
cards.text: Inherit publicly from `enable_shared_from_this<T>`. `shared_from_this()` shares the existing block.

slides.title: Pick the pointer by ownership
slides.takeaway: `shared_ptr` everywhere is not a design: it hides who owns what and invites cycles.

items.myth: "`weak_ptr` keeps the object alive until the weak count is 0."
items.truth: The object dies at strong 0. Only the control block waits.

items.myth: "`lock()` gives a raw pointer to the memory."
items.truth: It returns a `shared_ptr` (temporary co-ownership), empty if expired.
It is the strong count of the observed object.
`weak_ptr` has no `->`, `*` or `get()`. It does not compile.

items.myth: "Make any link weak: one weak link breaks the cycle."
items.truth: It must be the non-owning (back) link, or ownership semantics change.
Raw is right for non-owning access with a guaranteed lifetime.

slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The code checks expired() before it calls lock().
Careful code, right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: In production the release comes from another thread, so this crashes once a week. Here it crashes every time.

slides.title: It checks `expired()` first. Safe?

slides.verdict_sub: Typically a segfault, nothing printed. UBSan: "member access within null pointer"
bullets: `expired()` said false, then the last owner was released.
`lock()` correctly returns an **empty** `shared_ptr`. It never throws.
Each call is atomic. The check-then-act sequence is not.

slides.title: `lock()` is the check
slides.takeaway: Test and own in one step. Use `expired()` only for cleanup, never as a guard for access.

text.hook:
To avoid a shared_ptr cycle, this callback captures the button by reference.
Problem solved?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: It avoids one bug by trading it for a worse one.

slides.title: No cycle here. Output?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC 11, -O0: printed `~Button` then a stale `ok`. ASan: stack-use-after-scope
bullets: `[&btn]` captures a reference to the **local variable**, not ownership.
At the closing brace `btn` dies, and with it the `Button`.
`cb()` reads a dead stack object and follows whatever pointer is there.
The cycle is gone, but a leak became a use-after-free.

slides.title: Capture a `weak_ptr` by value
slides.takeaway: No cycle, no dangling: the callback observes, and `lock()` tells it when the object is gone.

text.hook:
Two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other.
Both owners call reset(). Someone in the room says "deadlock".

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: One of the wrong answers is a word every interviewer is listening for.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Counts never reach 0, so no destructor runs
bullets: LeakSanitizer reports it only as "Indirect leak".
slides.wrong: "Deadlock: each waits for the other to be destroyed"

slides.title: Make the back link a `weak_ptr`
bullets: Nothing waits in a cycle, so it is not a deadlock. Nothing is deleted, so no double delete.
slides.takeaway: The destructors' side effects are lost too: sockets never closed, files never flushed.

text.hook:
enable_shared_from_this, and an object on the stack.
A common answer: "shared_from_this() returns nullptr".

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: C++17 changed what this line does.

slides.title: C++17. What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Guaranteed since C++17. Before C++17: undefined behaviour
bullets: It needs an existing `shared_ptr` owner. A stack object has none.
Same failure in the constructor (no owner yet) and the destructor (count already 0).
It never creates a new control block, and it compiles fine.
`weak_from_this()` (C++17) never throws: it returns an empty `weak_ptr`.
slides.wrong: "It returns nullptr if the object is not shared"

slides.title: Enforce the owner with a factory
slides.takeaway: Private constructor + `static create()` returning `shared_ptr`, then `start()` registers callbacks.
